notes.purpose: Agenda and how it connects to the rest of the day.
notes.talk_track: We go first so you see the end state. This afternoon you build an agent, write benchmarks and a metric view. Those are exactly the pieces this pipeline promotes and watches.

notes.purpose: Most teams version only the left side. Both sides change answers.
notes.talk_track: Open the dev agent and show both halves. If prod gets a new instruction but not the metric view change it depends on, prod answers differently from dev. So both halves have to move together, through the same pipeline.
evidence: Live: dev agent in the demo workspace
notes.transition: So what moves, and what changes per environment?
notes.likely_question: Where do metric views live? In Unity Catalog, next to the tables. The agent just points at them.

slides.title: What moves, what changes per environment

data: SQL files, run by a bundle job
Users can chat; only the pipeline can edit

notes.purpose: The mental model for promotion.
notes.talk_track: Three kinds of things in one bundle. Resources are what the bundle creates and owns: the agent, the warehouse, the job. SQL is what the job runs: the tables and metric views. Variables are what change per environment: which catalog and schema. The catalogs and schemas already exist; your platform team owns those. Bundles are the recommended path; the APIs and Terraform work too, but you end up writing the plumbing yourself.
notes.transition: Here is the pipeline that does the promotion.
notes.likely_question: Can the catalog name differ per environment? Yes, that is exactly what the variables are for.

slides.title: What's in the bundle
code:
databricks.yml                 # variables and targets
resources/
  warehouse.yml                # resource: SQL warehouse
  build_context.job.yml        # resource: job that runs the SQL
  taxi_agent.genie.yml         # resource: the Genie agent
src/sql/
  01_tables.sql                # SQL: tables
  02_metric_views.sql          # SQL: metric views
slides.caption: Resources: the bundle creates and owns them. SQL: a job runs it. Variables: what changes per environment.

notes.purpose: Orient them in the repo before the snippets.
notes.talk_track: Three kinds of files. Resources are objects the bundle creates and keeps in sync: the warehouse, the job, the agent. SQL is DDL that the job runs, because bundles have no table or metric view resource. Variables are the per-environment values. Catalogs and schemas are not in here; they already exist.
notes.transition: Start with the variables.
notes.likely_question: Why not a table resource? Bundles do not have one; tables come from your pipelines or, as here, SQL a job runs.

slides.title: Variables per environment
code:
variables:
  catalog:
    description: Catalog holding the agent's data
  schema:
    description: Schema holding the agent's data
  consumer_group:
    default: users

targets:
  dev:
    mode: development
    variables: {schema: genie_demo_dev}
  prod:
    mode: production
    variables: {schema: genie_demo_prod}

# In a pipeline, override at deploy time:
databricks bundle deploy -t prod \
  --var catalog=analytics

# Or per machine, not committed:
# .databricks/bundle/prod/variable-overrides.json
{"catalog": "analytics"}

# A catalog per environment works the same
# way: set catalog per target instead.
slides.caption: ${var.schema} anywhere in the bundle becomes genie_demo_dev or genie_demo_prod, depending on the target.

notes.purpose: Variables are the only thing that differs between dev and prod.
notes.talk_track: One set of files, two targets. This demo promotes between two schemas in one catalog; a catalog per environment is the same variable, set per target. A pipeline can override with --var, and a developer can keep local values in a file that is not committed.
notes.transition: Now the resources, starting with the warehouse.
notes.likely_question: Can targets be different workspaces? Yes, add a workspace host per target; same files.

slides.title: Resource: the SQL warehouse
code:
resources:
  sql_warehouses:
    genie_wh:
      name: genie-agents-${bundle.target}
      cluster_size: 2X-Small
      warehouse_type: PRO
      enable_serverless_compute: true
      auto_stop_mins: 10
      max_num_clusters: 1
      permissions:
        - level: CAN_USE
          group_name: ${var.consumer_group}
slides.caption: One warehouse per target, sized and permissioned in code. Other resources reference it as ${resources.sql_warehouses.genie_wh.id}.

notes.purpose: The agent's compute is part of the deployment.
notes.talk_track: Each environment gets its own small serverless warehouse with auto stop. Users get CAN_USE so the agent can run their queries. Nobody clicks this together in the UI, and prod's warehouse is the same shape as dev's.
notes.transition: The tables and metric views come next, as SQL.
notes.likely_question: Can we share one warehouse across agents? Yes; reference an existing one with a variable instead of a resource.

slides.title: SQL: tables and metric views
code:
USE CATALOG IDENTIFIER(:catalog);
USE SCHEMA IDENTIFIER(:schema);

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW trip_metrics
WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS $$
version: 1.1
source: trips
dimensions:
  - name: pickup_zip
    expr: pickup_zip
measures:
  - name: total_revenue
    expr: SUM(fare_amount)
$$;
slides.caption: :catalog and :schema are SQL parameters the job passes in. The same files build dev and prod.

notes.purpose: Tables and metric views are DDL, versioned next to the agent.
notes.talk_track: Bundles have no metric view resource, so the definition lives as SQL. Notice the source is just trips: after USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, the same file works in any environment. In a real project the tables come from your pipelines; the metric view usually lives here with the agent.
notes.transition: A job runs these files.
notes.likely_question: Why parameters and not ${var.catalog}? The SQL file is uploaded as-is; the job passes the values as parameters.

slides.title: Resource: the job that runs the SQL
code:
resources:
  jobs:
    build_context:
      tasks:
        - task_key: tables
          sql_task:
            warehouse_id: ${resources.sql_warehouses.genie_wh.id}
            file:
              path: ../src/sql/01_tables.sql
            parameters:
              catalog: ${var.catalog}
              schema: ${var.schema}
        - task_key: metric_views
          depends_on: [{task_key: tables}]
          sql_task: ...   # same, 02_metric_views.sql
slides.caption: Variables flow into SQL as job parameters. Tables run first, then metric views.

notes.purpose: How the SQL gets applied in each environment.
notes.talk_track: The job is a bundle resource, so it deploys with everything else. It runs on the bundle's warehouse and passes the target's catalog and schema into the SQL. The pipeline runs it right after deploy.
notes.transition: Last, the agent itself.
notes.likely_question: Could this be a Lakeflow pipeline instead? Yes, if your tables are built by one already.

slides.title: Resource: the Genie agent
slides.caption: The whole agent definition is inline, so ${var.catalog} resolves inside it. Users get CAN_RUN; only the pipeline can edit.

notes.purpose: The agent is code, and it points at the variables and the warehouse.
notes.talk_track: The definition is exported from the dev agent, then the catalog and schema are replaced with variables. It has to be inline in the YAML; variables do not resolve in a separate JSON file. It references the bundle's warehouse by resource id.
notes.transition: Now the pipeline that ties it together.
notes.likely_question: How do UI edits get back into this file? make pull exports the dev agent and rewrites it with variables.

slides.title: The pipeline: five steps
slides.body:
Standards check: description, benchmarks, instructions, a metric view, no hardcoded names
Deploy the bundle: warehouse, job, agent
Run the job: tables, then metric views
Smoke test: ask prod one real question
Benchmark gate: run the benchmarks, stop below 80% (Beta API)

notes.purpose: The core of Part 1.
notes.talk_track: Show the Azure DevOps pipeline file, then run the same steps from the terminal: make release T=prod. Then the bad-change beat: add 'always exclude trips under 1 mile', which sounds reasonable. The gate drops to 50% and stops the release. Revert, and it passes.
evidence: Fallback: captured output in the repo's docs folder
notes.transition: A few things we learned building this.
notes.likely_question: Does the benchmark gate cost much? It runs the benchmark questions on your warehouse, so a few minutes of warehouse time.

slides.title: Four things worth knowing
slides.body:
Put the agent definition inline in the bundle so variables resolve
Create metric views before the agent; Genie rejects missing tables
Deploy into a restricted folder, not Shared, or everyone can edit prod
Business logic in a metric view protects answers from bad prompt edits

notes.purpose: Practical gotchas from building the demo, so they skip the trial and error.
notes.talk_track: Each of these we hit ourselves. The last one is the best argument for metric views: an instruction saying fares are stored in cents changed nothing, because Genie used the governed measure.
notes.transition: That gets one agent to prod. Now imagine fifty.
notes.likely_question: Does bundle generate work for pulling UI edits? Yes, the repo has a make pull that turns UI edits into a clean diff.

notes.purpose: The thesis of the hour: best practices make one agent good; the platform keeps fifty good.
notes.talk_track: Everything this afternoon is a best practice for one developer. None of it tells you which of your agents got worse last night. That is what this half is about.
notes.transition: Here are the signals you already have.
notes.likely_question: Who owns the platform side? Usually the same team that owns the pipeline. One ops setup watches every agent team's agents.

slides.title: Signals you already have
columns:
Run by API on a schedule
Results stored centrally
(Beta)

Thumbs up and down
from every conversation
No user names stored

SQL per agent: errors, speed
Who edited a prod agent
Genie spend by surface

notes.purpose: Where the data comes from. No new tooling to buy.
notes.talk_track: Open the Agent Fleet Health dashboard. Fleet Maintenance was healthy for weeks, then its pass rate dropped and thumbs-down climbed five days ago. That history is synthetic and labeled; the Taxi agent is live. Reading every user's conversations is an admin decision for you to make.
evidence: Seeded demo history is flagged synthetic
notes.transition: Signals only help if something acts on them.
notes.likely_question: Can we see who asked what? The API allows it; this design deliberately stores only questions and ratings.

slides.title: Alerts and automation
slides.body:
Re-test agents automatically when a table or metric view they read changes
Alerts: pass rate drops, thumbs-down rises, SQL failures, prod edited outside the pipeline
Thumbs-down questions go to a review list; a person decides the fix
Fixes go back through a pull request and the same gate
Metadata changes go through review too (Context Hub)

notes.purpose: The closed loop.
notes.talk_track: Live: write to the prod trips table; the re-test job fires about two minutes later and only re-tests agents that read that table. Show the review list. Benchmarks measure; they do not teach, so a person decides whether a thumbs-down becomes a new benchmark or an instruction fix. Two minutes of Context Hub: propose column descriptions for the trips table, approve, apply, re-test.
evidence: Live: Context Hub, a reference app you adopt and own
notes.transition: One more signal people always ask about: cost.
notes.likely_question: Is Context Hub a product? No, it is a reference app you can deploy and own.

slides.title: Cost, honestly
slides.body:
Billing shows Genie spend by surface: Genie One, agents, code
It does not split spend by individual agent
Warehouse time per agent is a good stand-in
Budget alerts can watch Genie spend for the account

notes.purpose: Set expectations correctly on cost attribution.
notes.talk_track: We looked: billing data tags Genie usage with the surface and channel, not the agent. So per-agent cost is a proxy from query history. Budget alerts are an account-admin setting.
notes.transition: So where do you start?
notes.likely_question: Will per-agent billing come? I would not plan around it; use the warehouse-time view for now.

slides.title: Where to start
slides.body:
Put one agent and its metric view in a bundle
Add the benchmark gate to your pipeline
Stand up the central ops tables and turn on three alerts
Decide who owns each agent and who approves changes
The demo repo has all of it, ready to copy

notes.purpose: Concrete next steps, smallest first.
notes.talk_track: Start with one agent. The gate is the highest-value single step. The ops layer can come once there are a handful of agents. Ownership is the decision that makes the rest work.
